solution:
Point P is the centre of the semicircular segment II, and it lies **on the line** containing the two straight segments I and III.

Straight segments: for every element of a straight segment, \(\mathrm{d}\vec{l}\) is parallel (or antiparallel) to the vector joining that element to P, so \(\mathrm{d}\vec{l} \times \hat{r} = 0\). Segments I and III therefore contribute **nothing**, whatever their length \(L\).

Semicircle: a circular arc of radius \(R\) subtending an angle \(\theta\) at its centre gives \(B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi R}\theta\). Here \(\theta = \pi\), so
\(B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi R}\times\pi = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4}\dfrac{I}{R}\)

This is the option printed third in the book's list.

The other three fail independently: \(\dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{I}{R}\) is the value for an arc of **one radian**, not a semicircle — short by a factor \(\pi\); \(\dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{I}{R^2}\) and \(\dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi}\) are **dimensionally impossible** for a magnetic field, carrying units of T m\(^{-1}\) and T m respectively. A direct numerical Biot-Savart integration with \(R = 0.5\) m, \(I = 3\) A and \(L = 2\) m returns \(1.88496 \times 10^{-6}\) T from the arc and exactly zero from each straight segment, matching \(\dfrac{\mu_0}{4}\dfrac{I}{R}\) to nine significant figures.

Ampere's circuital law states \(\displaystyle\oint \vec{B}\cdot\mathrm{d}\vec{l} = \mu_0 I_{enclosed}\), where \(I_{enclosed}\) counts only current that **passes through** the Amperian loop, with a sign fixed by the right-hand rule applied to the loop's own sense of traversal.

Case (b): the conductor runs past the loop without threading it, so no current passes through any surface bounded by the loop. Hence \(I_{enclosed} = 0\) and the integral is **zero**. That alone eliminates the two alternatives that give a non-zero value for case b.

Case (a): the conductor does thread the loop, so the magnitude is \(\mu_0 I\). The arrow drawn on the loop runs anticlockwise as seen by the reader, so by the right-hand rule the loop's positive normal points **out of the page**, towards the reader; the wire, however, is drawn passing in front of the loop on the left and behind it on the right, so the current threads the loop going **away from** the reader. Current and positive normal are antiparallel, so \(I_{enclosed} = -I\) and the integral is \(-\mu_0 I\).

The pair is therefore \(-\mu_0 I\), 0. The alternative \(\mu_0 I\), 0 is the trap for a student who gets the enclosure right and drops the sign.

Take \(\hat{x}\) along the axis, \(\hat{y}\) upward in the plane of the page and \(\hat{z}\) out of the page. The proton has \(\vec{v} = v\hat{x}\); the field is directed into the paper, so \(\vec{B} = -B\hat{z}\).

\(\vec{F} = q\,\vec{v}\times\vec{B} = q(v\hat{x})\times(-B\hat{z}) = -qvB\,(\hat{x}\times\hat{z}) = -qvB(-\hat{y}) = +qvB\,\hat{y}\)

The force on the (positively charged) proton is therefore along the **positive \(y\)** direction. It stays perpendicular to \(\vec{v}\) at every instant, so the proton turns along a circular arc at constant speed, curving **upward, towards the positive \(y\) axis**.

The three alternatives fail outright. Continuing along the positive \(x\) axis requires zero force, but \(\vec{v}\perp\vec{B}\) gives the maximum possible magnetic force. Bending towards the negative \(y\) axis has the deflection the wrong way round — that is the path of a negative charge, or of a proton in a field directed out of the page. A sinusoidal path needs a restoring force that reverses sign along the path, whereas a uniform magnetic field of constant magnitude produces a constant-speed circular arc.

The force on a straight current-carrying rod in a uniform field is \(\vec{F} = I\,\vec{L}\times\vec{B}\).

Magnitude: at the equator the field is horizontal and points south to north, while the current flows west to east, so \(\vec{L}\perp\vec{B}\) and
\(F = BIL = (1.3\times10^{-4})(15)(1) = 1.95\times10^{-3}\) N \(= 19.5\times10^{-4}\) N \(\approx 20\times10^{-4}\) N

Direction: take \(\hat{x}\) east, \(\hat{y}\) north and \(\hat{z}\) vertically up. Then \(\vec{F} = IL\hat{x}\times B\hat{y} = ILB\,(\hat{x}\times\hat{y}) = ILB\,\hat{z}\) — **vertically upward**.

The answer is \(20\times10^{-4}\) N, upward.

The alternatives are each excluded: the value \(14\times10^{-4}\) N follows from no combination of the given data (it would need \(I \approx 10.8\) A or \(B \approx 0.93\times10^{-4}\) T), and "downward" reverses the cross product.

The magnetic force \(\vec{F} = q\,\vec{v}\times\vec{B}\) is by construction perpendicular to \(\vec{v}\). The rate at which it does work on the particle is
\(P = \vec{F}\cdot\vec{v} = q(\vec{v}\times\vec{B})\cdot\vec{v} = 0\)
because \(\vec{v}\times\vec{B}\) is orthogonal to \(\vec{v}\).

A magnetic field therefore **never does work** on a moving charge. It can change the direction of \(\vec{v}\) — here bending the particle into a circle, since \(\vec{v}\perp\vec{B}\) — but never its magnitude. The speed, and hence the kinetic energy \(\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2\), stays **unchanged**.

The other options each require the magnetic force to do work: "get reduced" and "increase" both need \(P \ne 0\), and "be reduced to zero" would require the particle to stop, which never happens — it circulates indefinitely at constant speed.
